prompt: Why does "take items in decreasing order of value per kilogram" solve the **fractional knapsack** optimally but not the **0/1 knapsack**?

options.text: Because fractional knapsack has fewer items
options.explanation: The item count is the same in both versions. The difference is whether an item can be split.

options.text: Because value-per-kilogram is computed incorrectly for whole items
options.explanation: The ratio is the same either way. The problem is what happens when the best-ratio item doesn't fill the bag neatly.

options.text: With fractions you can always fill leftover room with part of the next-best item; with whole items, a high-ratio item can leave a gap that wastes room, so a combination of lower-ratio items may be better
options.explanation: Correct. In the lesson's example greedy takes D (5 kg) and wastes 1 kg of the 7, scoring 8; B + C fill all 7 kg for 9.

options.text: Greedy is optimal for both; the 0/1 version just needs sorting by weight instead
options.explanation: Sorting by weight is not generally exact either. A polynomial-time rule solving all binary-encoded 0/1 knapsack instances would imply that every problem whose answers can be checked in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time, which is unresolved.

workedExample:
1. Fractional: sort by ratio, take whole items while they fit, then a fraction of the next. Any room not filled by a high-ratio item is filled by the next best ratio, until the bag is full or the available material is exhausted. An exchange argument proves optimality.
2. 0/1, weight limit 7: items A(1, 1), B(3, 4), C(4, 5), D(5, 7).
   - Greedy: D (ratio 1.40) → 2 kg left. B (3 kg) and C (4 kg) don't fit. A fits → total 8, 1 kg wasted.
   - Optimum: B + C = 7 kg, value 9.
3. The wasted kilogram is what greedy can't recover from, and why this greedy rule fails; DP over the weight limit is one exact alternative.

prompt:
0/1 knapsack, weight limit 5, items (weight, value) added one per row. The finished table (columns are weight limits 0 to 5):

```
items   0 1 2 3 4 5
none    0 0 0 0 0 0
(2,3)   0 0 3 3 3 3
(3,4)   0 0 3 4 4 7
(4,5)   0 0 3 4 5 7
(5,6)   0 0 3 4 5 7
```

Walking back from the bottom-right cell, which items are in the best packing?

options.text: (5, 6) alone, because its row is last and it fills the bag exactly
options.explanation: Its row has the same value at limit 5 as the row above (7 and 7), so adding (5, 6) changed nothing: it was not taken.
Those weigh 6, over the limit. Also, the (4, 5) row equals the row above it at limit 5, so it was not taken.

options.text: All four, because every row reaches at least 3
options.explanation: A row's value only shows the best packing using items up to that row. An item is taken only where its row improves on the row above at the current limit.
Correct. At limit 5 the value first changes in the (3, 4) row (3 → 7), so take it and continue at limit 2. There the (2, 3) row improves 0 → 3, so take it too. Total weight 5, value 7.

workedExample:
1. Start at the bottom-right: 7, using all four items with limit 5.
2. Compare each row with the row above at the current limit. Equal means the item was skipped; different means it was taken.
3. (5, 6): 7 equals 7 above, so skip. (4, 5): 7 equals 7 above, so skip.
4. (3, 4): 7 differs from 3 above, so take it and subtract its weight: continue at limit 2.
5. (2, 3) at limit 2: 3 differs from 0 above, so take it and continue at limit 0.
6. Result: (2, 3) + (3, 4), weight 5, value 7. Reconstruction needs the full table (or stored choices), which is why the single-array version in the next unit can give the value but not the items.
